name: Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? On Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Shaokun Zhang, Ming Yin, Jieyu Zhang, Jiale Liu, Zhiguang Han, Jingyang Zhang, Beibin Li, Chi Wang, Huazheng Wang, Yiran Chen, Qingyun Wu (lead affiliations: Pennsylvania State University; co-authors from University of Washington, Duke University, Microsoft Research / AG2, Oregon State University)
venue: ICML 2025 (Forty-second International Conference on Machine Learning), Spotlight; also arXiv:2505.00212
reflection_type: learned-critic-model | multi-agent-debate (LLM-as-judge for failure attribution). The work uses LLM-as-judge methods that critique a completed multi-agent failure trace to attribute the responsible agent and decisive error step; it is an analysis/benchmark of attribution (a form of post-hoc self-reflection / critic) rather than an in-loop self-correction method.
feedback_source: self-generated (LLM judge reasoning over the failure log) plus an optional ground-truth-oracle signal: experiments are run under a 'With Ground Truth' setting (final query answer available to the judge) and a 'Without Ground Truth' setting; human expert annotations provide the evaluation ground truth.
iteration_structure: single-shot (All-at-Once: judge sees full log once) and iterative (Step-by-Step: incremental step-wise judging until first error; Binary Search: halving the log iteratively to localize the step). A Hybrid method runs All-at-Once then Step-by-Step sequentially.
reflection_object: action trajectory / conversation log of an LLM multi-agent system. The methods reflect on a completed multi-agent failure log to localize (1) the failure-responsible agent and (2) the decisive error step; nothing in the multi-agent system's content, prompts, weights, or skills is modified by the attribution itself.
requires_training: none for the three evaluated attribution methods (all are prompting-based LLM-as-judge with frozen models, GPT-4o primary; open models Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B/72B-Instruct are also used as judges without fine-tuning in the main experiments). The released repo/benchmark is positioned to support future training (e.g., reward models / fine-tuned attributors), but the paper itself reports no weight updates.
reward_or_critic_model: self-as-judge (an LLM is the attribution critic). No trained reward model is used; the work explicitly notes that the resulting decisive-error signal could later serve as a reward for RL or as feedback for agent self-improvement, and contrasts with process reward models (Math-Shepherd, ProcessBench) which target single-LLM reasoning rather than multi-agent attribution.
distillation_target: none. The reflection (failure attribution) is not distilled into a reusable artifact within the paper; the reusable output is the Who&When benchmark and the attribution method recipes, not a learned skill/memory/weight artifact.
emergent_vs_engineered: prompt/scaffold-engineered. The three attribution strategies (All-at-Once, Step-by-Step, Binary Search) and the Hybrid combination are hand-designed prompting scaffolds; the paper finds that engineering a reasoning mechanism into the prompt helps more than swapping to RL-emergent reasoning models (o1/R1).
memory_type: none (the attribution methods are stateless judges over a single failure log per instance; no persistent memory/skill library is built). The Who&When dataset itself is a static corpus of annotated failure logs.
memory_persistence: within-episode (judgment is performed per failure log / per task instance; no cross-episode or cross-session memory is maintained by the methods).
error_localization_granularity: agent-level (multi-agent) and step-level. The task is defined as jointly identifying the failure-responsible agent (Who) and the decisive error step (When); evaluation uses Agent-Level Accuracy, Step-Level Accuracy, and Step-Level Accuracy with Tolerance (+/-1 to +/-5 steps).
intra_task_vs_inter_task: intra-task analysis at the single-data-instance level (localize the failure within one task's trace). The paper also notes the three methods are more effective at extracting statistical (dataset-level) conclusions than precise single-instance attribution, but it does not transfer learned experience across tasks.
failure_recovery_vs_avoidance: post-hoc-revision / diagnosis. Attribution is performed after the multi-agent system has already failed; it produces a debugging signal rather than recovering mid-trajectory or avoiding future failures within the studied pipeline.
task_domains: general agentic problem-solving / multi-agent systems debugging; underlying queries are real-world web/tool-use and reasoning tasks (web navigation, file handling, information seeking, QA/reasoning) drawn from GAIA and AssistantBench.
benchmarks: Who&When (the introduced benchmark: 127 LLM multi-agent systems, 184 annotated failure tasks; Algorithm-Generated subset via CaptainAgent/AG2 and Hand-Crafted subset via Magnetic-One). Source queries: GAIA and AssistantBench. Related/contrast benchmarks discussed: ProcessBench, DevAI.
headline_result: On Who&When, the best automated failure-attribution method reaches 53.5% accuracy at identifying the failure-responsible agent (All-at-Once, averaged across the with/without-ground-truth settings) but only 14.2% accuracy at pinpointing the decisive failure step (Step-by-Step); some methods (e.g., All-at-Once on step-level) fall below the random baseline. SOTA reasoning models (OpenAI o1, DeepSeek R1) do not reach practical usability.
baselines: Random baseline (Agent-Level 29.10% algorithm-generated / 12.00% hand-crafted; Step-Level 19.06% / 4.16%); the three attribution methods compared against each other (All-at-Once vs Step-by-Step vs Binary Search) and against a Hybrid combination; judge-model ablations across GPT-4o, GPT-4, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B/72B-Instruct, and reasoning models OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek R1.
gains_vs_baseline: All-at-Once beats Step-by-Step on agent-level accuracy by ~19.13% and ~20.69% (with ground truth) and ~25.1% and ~20.69% (without ground truth); all three methods exceed the random baseline on agent-level accuracy, confirming the task is nontrivial. Conversely on step-level accuracy Step-by-Step is best (top in 3 of 4 cases) while All-at-Once can fall below random. The Hybrid (Step-by-Step & All-at-Once) achieves the best of both: 57.02% agent-level and 12.28% step-level on hand-crafted systems, vs Binary Search 43.97%/6.90%, All-at-Once 57.02%/4.39%, Step-by-Step 35.96%/7.90%. Providing ground truth improves all methods on all metrics over the no-ground-truth setting.
compute_cost_profile: Inference-only (no training). Token cost varies sharply by method on hand-crafted systems: All-at-Once ~17,106 tokens (cheapest, single pass), Binary Search ~34,659 tokens, Step-by-Step ~87,720 tokens, and the Hybrid method ~149,177 tokens (highest, since it runs two algorithms sequentially). Whole-dataset evaluation across many models was limited to hand-crafted systems due to high token/compute cost.
known_limitations: (1) Even the best method is far from practically usable, especially at step-level (best ~14.2%, near 0% when logs are longest). (2) Performance degrades sharply as failure-log/context length increases (Levels 1-5: 5-17 up to 93-130 steps), converging toward 0% at the maximum length due to a long-context 'space-in-the-needle' retrieval problem. (3) Methods trade off: large-receptive-field (All-at-Once) is good for Who but bad for When; incremental (Step-by-Step) is the reverse. (4) Stronger reasoning models (o1, R1) do not reliably beat GPT-4o (R1 underperforms GPT-4o in 3 of 4 cases). (5) The formulation assumes a single deterministic failure-responsible agent and one decisive error step, which later work (e.g., 'Rethinking Failure Attribution', 2026) critiques as too rigid and not capturing cascading/multi-cause failures or attribution reasoning. (6) Study is single-data-instance level; dataset-level statistical attribution is more reliable than per-instance.
oracle_or_external_feedback_dependency: task-dependent on oracle access: in the 'With Ground Truth' setting the final query answer (a partial oracle) is available and measurably boosts all methods on all metrics; in the 'Without Ground Truth' setting only the running log is used (intrinsic self-verify), and accuracy drops. The headline 53.5%/14.2% numbers are averaged over both settings, so the method is not purely intrinsic.
self_correction_efficacy: task-dependent / requires-oracle. As a debugging signal the methods are net-positive over random for agent identification, but for step localization the strongest single method (All-at-Once) can be net-negative (below random); reliable use benefits from ground-truth labels and from combining methods (Hybrid). The paper frames attribution as a feedback signal for downstream self-improvement rather than demonstrating closed-loop self-correction gains.
calibration_effect: not-measured (the paper reports accuracy of attribution, not confidence calibration of the judged systems).
failure_attribution_capability: attributes-responsible-agent and attributes-failing-step. The work formalizes joint Who (failure-responsible agent) and When (decisive error step) attribution over LLM multi-agent traces, with a causal/counterfactual notion of the 'decisive error' step that, if corrected, would change the outcome.
failure_mode_addressed: Targets localization of the single decisive error in multi-agent cooperation that causes system-level task failure (the agent and step whose error propagates to failure). It exposes attribution-side failure modes such as long-context retrieval failure ('space-in-the-needle'), inability to localize within long traces, and the difficulty of disambiguating multiple erring agents. It is complementary to MAST-style taxonomies (Cemri et al. 2025) but does not itself classify the 14 MAST failure modes; it provides agent/step localization rather than a failure-mode taxonomy.
dataset_or_benchmark_released: Yes. Who&When benchmark: failure logs from 127 LLM multi-agent systems with 184 fine-grained annotated failure tasks (each labeled with failure-responsible agent, decisive error step, and a natural-language explanation), split into Algorithm-Generated (CaptainAgent/AG2) and Hand-Crafted (Magnetic-One) subsets, built on GAIA and AssistantBench queries. Released on GitHub (ag2ai/Agents_Failure_Attribution) and Hugging Face (Kevin355/Who_and_When), MIT-licensed.
builds_on: CaptainAgent / AG2 (AutoGen) for algorithm-generated systems (Song et al. 2024); Magnetic-One generalist multi-agent system (Fourney et al. 2024); GAIA (Mialon et al. 2023) and AssistantBench (Yoran et al. 2024) for source queries; LLM-as-judge / LLM-as-evaluator line (Zhuge et al. 2024 DevAI; van Schaik & Pugh 2024); Reflexion-style self-reflection (Shinn et al. 2024); process reward / step-error-localization work (Math-Shepherd Wang et al. 2023; ProcessBench; Lightman et al. 2023).
extended_by_or_inspired: Subsequent automated failure-attribution work that adopts or critiques the Who&When formulation, e.g., 'Rethinking Failure Attribution in Multi-Agent Systems: A Multi-Perspective Benchmark and Evaluation' (2026, arXiv:2603.25001), 'Intention-behavior consistency-based automated failure attribution for LLM-driven multi-agent systems' (ScienceDirect 2026), and follow-ups by Zhang et al. 2025a/b, Kong et al. 2025, Ma et al. 2025, and West et al. 2025; complements MAST (Cemri et al. 2025).
citation_count: 90 (Semantic Scholar, as of June 2026; 22 influential citations)
reasoning_model_native: Partially evaluated, not native. The method is model-agnostic prompting; the paper explicitly tests reasoning models OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek R1 as judges and finds they do NOT reliably outperform GPT-4o (R1 underperforms GPT-4o in 3 of 4 cases; o1 not consistently better), concluding that built-in reasoning models alone do not solve failure attribution.
sample_efficiency: Not a training method, so no trials-to-gain measure; cost is per-instance inference. Token-cost ranking per hand-crafted instance: All-at-Once ~17.1K (1 pass), Binary Search ~34.7K, Step-by-Step ~87.7K, Hybrid ~149.2K tokens.
